lead: Plan in four stages, check all the way; pilotage is the same at close range, with every number ready before the entrance. The electronics serve both, if you know what each cannot see.

sections.title: Four stages and a way out

fig.title: The four stages
lines: Appraisal: charts, pilot, tides, forecasts
Planning: tracks, waypoints, times, plan B
Execution: latest forecast, decide, brief
Monitoring: fix, compare with the plan, act

blocks.p: SOLAS V asks every vessel for a plan, and a radar reflector where practicable. Work timings backwards: latest departure = the **earlier** forecast of bad weather − margin − passage time; likewise back from a tidal gate. Landfall: raise a light before dawn, enter after it. Per stage: a **port of refuge**, safe in the forecast wind at any tide, and a port with a hospital. Fuel by dipstick: passage + diversion + reserve; bottled water for the passage plus spare days. Handing over: the plan's changes, the defects, the crew.

fig.title: Latest departure
lines: Crossing 120 M at 8 kn: 15 h
Front: model A Sat 1800, model B Sat 1200
Rule: in harbour 6 h before the earlier one

blocks.p: Cross lanes at right angles at a steady heading and speed, clear of the **precautionary area** where ships turn, and keep waypoints off the point where they all alter. A platform's 500 m zone is closed to you; a wind farm at night hides small craft among its echoes.

fig.note: A: both lanes at right angles · B: where ships turn

sections.title: Somebody is always checking
refs: Passage planning — watches and night orders

blocks.p: Lanes and landfall where the crew is fresh and it is light; sleep before the night, not after. A lone watchkeeper under autopilot needs a **watch alarm**. Night orders never delay avoiding action: at close quarters act, then call. Fix more often as dangers close, so you cannot reach one between fixes; a fix well off the EP means stream, sensor or plot is wrong. A saved track is no log: no weather or decisions, and it dies with the power.

fig.title: Night orders
lines: Fix every 30 min offshore
Every 6 min within 3 M of a danger
Call me: CPA under 1 M, or any doubt
Close quarters: act first, then call
Watch alarm on; log every hour

sections.title: Ready before the entrance
refs: Pilotage — an unlit anchorage by radar

fig.title: In the plan
lines: Tide = draught + ½ swell + margin − depth
Bridge: clearance + HAT − tide ≥ air draught
Clearing bearings; wheel-over points
Abort point: the last place to turn away
VTS: name, position, intention, ETA; listen

blocks.p: A **clearing bearing** on a charted mark fences off a danger; deeper water at night and in a swell.

fig.note: Night, swell: keep seaward of C — light bearing ≤ 314°

blocks.p: Start a big turn early: **wheel-over** distance = turning radius × tan(half the turn). Leading lights hold a dredged cut's axis; a white sector may be wider than your water. Mark the **abort point**; where you cannot turn inside, reverse in. Without GNSS **aim off** to one side of the harbour; in an unlit bay fix by radar ranges off steep points and the sounder. Three vertical reds: no entry; the yellow beside them exempts only named craft. VTS traffic information is not control. In fog let the ferry clear first, and be able to stop within half the visibility.

fig.note: Three reds: no entry · the yellow frees named craft

sections.title: What paints
refs: Radar — parallel indexing with a stream
Radar and the plotter — overlay offset

blocks.p: Range = speed of radio waves × echo time ÷ 2; the picture ends at the horizon. Range to the near edge of an echo is sharp; bearing is smeared by the beam width: fix by ranges.

fig.title: Radar horizon
lines: ≈ 2.2 × (√h₁ + √h₂) M, heights in metres
Scanner 9 m, cliff 64 m: 2.2 × 11 = 24 M
Ship's bridge 30 m: 2.2 × (3 + 5.5) ≈ 19 M
Her AIS from a high aerial reaches further

fig.title: Setting up the picture
lines: Tune, then gain up to a faint speckle
Sea clutter: leave a little showing
Rain control only to look into a squall
Long scale to warn, short for small craft
Long scale ≥ closing speed × warning time

blocks.p: Heavy rain hides what lies behind it. A **guard zone** misses an echo that first paints inside it; an arc at a close ship's range is side lobes. Yaw to clear a blind sector; an active enhancer high up makes you seen. A **racon** paints a Morse flash outward: range to its near end. A **SART** paints twelve dots, the casualty at the nearest. **Parallel index**: a line parallel to your ground track, on a stabilised north-up display. **Clearing range**: a VRM ring round a cliff that echoes, at the hidden danger's reach plus margin. No true trail: stopped. Overlay offset evenly all round: doubt the position.

fig.note: The reef gives no echo: keep the cliff outside 1.0 M

sections.title: Her CPA, her true course
refs: Radar plotting — true and relative motion
Radar plotting — the alteration for a CPA
Radar plotting — a target that alters

blocks.p: Plot an echo twice. The line through the plots, extended, is her **relative motion**: it passes you at the CPA; distance left along it ÷ relative speed = TCPA. Steady bearing, closing range: collision. Two targets: the earlier CPA first.

fig.note: Relative motion · 3.2 M to the CPA at 15 kn: 13 min

blocks.p: Relative motion + your own course and speed = her true course and speed. After you alter or slow, redraw from the last plot: her true vector minus your new one. A bend in the plot means she has altered: start again from the bend.

**ARPA** draws this, with limits. Read the CPA, not where the true vector points. Vectors take three minutes to settle. A heading error skews true vectors, not CPA and TCPA. Close-passing echoes can swap. Ground-stabilised vectors show track over the ground; in a cross-stream her lights disagree, so judge aspect sea-stabilised.

sections.title: What she says of herself
refs: AIS — what it does not show
AIS — what it shows and what it does not

blocks.p: AIS says what a ship's GNSS and crew report, over VHF. Many fishing boats, yachts, warships and tows have none, and the status is typed by hand. Plot an echo with no AIS like any other; two echoes in step under one name are tug and tow: never pass between. **Class B** sends 2 W every 30 seconds and may be filtered off a busy display. A **virtual aid** exists only on the screen: plot the danger on paper.

head: MMSI
Device
rows: AIS-SART, no radar dots. ACTIVE: go, alert the MRCC; TEST: log it
MOB beacon: a person in the water

sections.title: One source is none
refs: GNSS — failure and what is left
Integrated electronics — single point of failure

blocks.p: High **HDOP**: poor satellite geometry, worse fix. SBAS sharpens the fix and flags faults, but jams too. **Jamming**: jumps, wild SOG, wrong clock, no fix. **Spoofing**: a smooth, confident, false position. Radar ranges and depths are independent: believe them, report it.

lines: Position jumps; radar, log and compass steady
Go by radar ranges, depth and DR

fig.title: GNSS lost
lines: Write down the last fix, its time and log
Start a DR; fix by radar ranges and depth
Gone: AIS and DSC positions, track steering
Still good: radar, compass, log, sounder
Backup: handheld GNSS, VHF, own batteries

blocks.p: One antenna for everything: a single point of failure. **Wind mode** follows the wind, not the compass; off-course alarm in gusts: reef; drive fault: hand steering, slow down. Below-keel sounder reading + draught = the depth to compare with the chart; offshore it shows fish as shoals. Log factor = true ÷ logged distance, at slack water. GNSS SOG and COG already hold the stream.
